name: Gua sha scraping

lead: Gua sha scraping is a hands-on technique from traditional Chinese medicine in which a smooth-edged tool is drawn along oiled skin in firm, one-directional strokes until red marks called sha appear. It is traditionally used on the back, neck and limbs for aches, tiredness and colds.

In beauty culture a lighter version is applied to the face and neck, where fans describe less puffiness, a more sculpted jawline and a fresher complexion. Clinical research on scraping is mostly from Chinese trials in conditions such as post-stroke spasticity; its use for appearance has not been tested in trials.

paras: Practitioners oil the skin and use a ceramic spoon, coin, jade or buffalo-horn tool with repeated strokes along muscles. Body scraping is done firmly until the marks (sha) appear; facial versions use lighter pressure and are often shared on social media as short routines. Marks from body work typically fade over days.

Nearly every body treatment leaves redness and bruising, and burns, dermatitis and blood in the urine have been reported, with rare serious cases including brain bleeding and skin injuries needing grafts. Unsterilised tools or broken skin raise infection concerns. Practitioners and clinicians generally advise people on blood thinners or with bleeding disorders to be cautious.

angle.text: Users apply a lighter version to the face and neck hoping for a leaner-looking contour and brighter skin, and the body version is used for muscle tightness that practitioners say affects posture and comfort. These effects are described by practitioners and users rather than measured in appearance trials.

lead: Gua sha scraping (Chinese: 刮痧) is a traditional practice in which a smooth-edged tool such as a ceramic spoon, coin, jade piece or water-buffalo horn is drawn firmly along oiled skin until small red petechiae, called sha, appear. It is used across East and Southeast Asia and also goes by names such as coining and spooning.[1]

In appearance culture the technique appears in two forms. The traditional body version aims at muscle tightness and fatigue, and practitioners say the temporary marks signal released stagnation. A gentler facial version spread widely through TikTok and beauty influencers in 2021 and 2022, where users describe it as a way to reduce puffiness, define the jaw and cheekbones and brighten skin.[1]

Published research is concentrated on body use in China; a 2026 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined scraping as an add-on to rehabilitation for spasticity after stroke.[2] Trials examining scraping for facial appearance have not been published.

paras: Practitioners apply oil or balm and use firm, one-directional strokes with a smooth edge along muscles or channels (meridians), continuing until petechiae appear. Pressure is lighter for facial work and firmer for musculoskeletal complaints. It is sometimes paired with fire cupping.[1]
The red or purple marks are called sha. In traditional theory, sha reflects wind or cold stagnating in the body, and raising it is thought to release the blockage.

Wikipedia links the idea of scraping-like treatment to the Shanghan Lun, a Chinese medical text from around 220 CE, with more formal use in the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644), when texts described it for sha syndromes.[1]

Facial gua sha became a social media trend in 2021 and 2022, with beauty influencers promoting it for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation, as reported by Hannah Seo in The New York Times in September 2022.[1] Related pages on this wiki cover the stone tools and neck routines.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of Chinese randomised trials, with a preclinical mechanistic synthesis, looked at gua sha as an adjunct to standard rehabilitation for spasticity after stroke and reported emerging data suggesting an adjunct antispastic effect.[2] No studies found on gua sha for facial appearance, skin tone or contour.

Wikipedia, citing Edzard Ernst and Mark Crislip among others, reports that critics say gua sha lacks high-quality clinical evidence and that the skin markers it relies on are misinterpreted physiological signs.[1] Practitioners and users, by contrast, report relief and relaxation.

Nearly every body treatment causes minor skin trauma, such as redness, bruising or dermatitis. Reported adverse events include burns and blood in the urine, and rare cases of brain bleeding and injuries requiring skin grafts (Vashi et al., 2018). Infection is a concern with unsterilised tools or open wounds.[1]
In Vietnamese, Cambodian and Indonesian diaspora families, marks on children have sometimes been mistaken for abuse; the 2001 Hong Kong film The Gua Sha Treatment dramatises such a case.[1]
